title: Checkpoint: Climates Past and Present
objective: After this level you can explain how sunlight, orbit, carbon and volcanoes have set Earth's climate from the ice ages to today.
summary: Orbital cycles pace the ice ages while carbon dioxide and ice amplify them. Across the chapter, carbon dioxide sets the long-term dial; volcanoes and seasons only nudge it for a while.

cards.headline: Chapter 8 finale: Earth's climate has dials that turn on very different clocks.
cards.body: A summer peaks several weeks late. A big eruption chills the world for one to three years. Orbital cycles swing over tens of thousands of years, and rock locks carbon away for millions. Here's how the dials fit together.

cards.headline: Pacemaker and amplifier
cards.body: Level 77's orbital cycles set the timing of the ice ages, but on their own they cause only small changes. Carbon dioxide and ice amplify them: as ice retreats, less sunlight is reflected, and rising carbon dioxide adds more warming. In Antarctic ice, temperature and carbon dioxide climbed together through most of the roughly 6,000-year warming out of the last ice age.

mascot.line: This is Levels 76 and 77 working together: the orbit sets the beat, and carbon and ice turn up the volume.

cards.headline: The same knob, every time
cards.body: Look back and carbon dioxide keeps turning up. It built up when volcanoes outran weathering and thawed Snowball Earth. It gets locked into limestone for millions of years. It rose and fell with the ice ages in Antarctic bubbles. Across 485 million years, it has been the dominant control on global temperature. A volcano's sulfur can chill the world for one to three years; carbon sets the long-term dial.

cards.headline: Chapter 8 complete
learned: How orbital cycles pace the ice ages while carbon dioxide and ice amplify them.
Why rock weathering and volcanoes work as a slow thermostat for carbon dioxide.
What ice cores, cap carbonates and loess reveal about Earth's past climates.
Why summer peaks late, and how to read a Köppen climate code.

questions.prompt: Match each climate dial with its clock.
questions.explanation: Summer peaks several weeks late, a big eruption chills the world for one to three years, orbital cycles swing over tens of thousands of years, and rock locks carbon away for millions.

questions.prompt: Why does shrinking ice make a warming stronger?

options.label: Meltwater releases heat stored in the ice
options.rationale: Melting takes in heat; it doesn't release it.

options.label: Less ice means less sunlight is reflected away
Melting ice triggers volcanic eruptions
options.rationale: Volcanoes aren't the link; less ice means less sunlight reflected.

options.label: Bare ground holds less carbon dioxide

questions.explanation: Ice reflects sunlight back to space, so as it retreats more sunlight is absorbed and the warming grows.

questions.prompt: Which clue in the rocks marks the sudden end of a Snowball Earth?

options.label: Loess spread across river valleys
options.rationale: That's ice-age dust from the last ice age.

options.label: Limestone cap carbonates lying on glacial deposits
Air bubbles sealed in Antarctic ice
options.rationale: Ice cores reach back 800,000 years, not 600 million.

options.label: Shale split into thin sheets
options.rationale: Shale is hardened mud, not a thaw marker.

questions.explanation: Cap carbonates, layered limestone (a calcium carbonate rock) or dolomite, sit right on the glacial deposits, recording the flip from ice to warmth.

questions.prompt: Why do the hottest weeks of summer arrive well after the longest day?

options.label: The Sun is closest to Earth in late July each year
options.rationale: Distance from the Sun isn't the reason; heat keeps building faster than it escapes.

options.label: Heat keeps piling up faster than it escapes
Summer rain stops cooling the ground
options.rationale: Rain isn't the reason; heat gain still outpaces heat loss.

options.label: The atmosphere thickens in midsummer
options.rationale: The air doesn't thicken; heat gain still outpaces heat loss.

questions.explanation: For weeks after the solstice, daytime heating still outpaces nighttime cooling, so warmth keeps building.

questions.prompt: In the Köppen code BWh, what does the W tell you?

options.label: The place is a true desert
Winter is the dry season
options.rationale: Lowercase w means a dry winter.

options.label: The place is a semiarid steppe

questions.explanation: In the dry B group, W marks a true desert (arid) and S a semiarid steppe; h adds hot.
